articles.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
articles.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.
articles.content:
Organic carbon has been confirmed in two ancient Martian rocks examined by NASA's Perseverance rover, adding an important new piece to the puzzle of whether Mars once supported life. Even more surprising, the material was found just beneath the planet's surface, where harsh conditions can destroy organic compounds.

The discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature. A potential biosignature is a substance or feature that could have formed through biological activity, although other explanations are possible. Now, research published in Science Advances provides definitive confirmation that the same two rocks, located in Mars' Bright Angel formation, contain organic carbon, an essential component of life. The findings also offer a clearer picture of the material's characteristics and how it may have been preserved.

The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.

NASA's Perseverance Rover Detects Complex Organic Carbon

To investigate the rocks, researchers used the Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument mounted on Perseverance's robotic arm. The instrument examined several rocks in the Bright Angel formation within Jezero crater, where the rover also collected a sample from a rock named "Cheyava Falls."

SHERLOC uses a technique called Raman spectroscopy, which shines laser light onto a material to identify and map its minerals and organic compounds without damaging the rock.

The measurements revealed macromolecular carbon (MMC), a form of carbon consisting of large, interconnected networks of carbon atoms. This type of material is also found in rocks on Earth and in meteorites. Importantly, it can form through biological activity or through chemical processes that do not involve life, so its presence alone cannot establish that Mars was once inhabited.

The surrounding geology offers additional clues about how the material reached these rocks. Billions of years ago, water flowed through a river channel into Jezero crater, carrying sediment that gradually settled on the bottom. Over time, those fine particles hardened into the mudstone formations Perseverance is now exploring.

Researchers detected the carbon within these ancient sediments and alongside carbonate and sulfate minerals that developed later as water altered the rocks. This distribution raises the possibility that organic material entered or formed within the rocks during at least two separate periods of Mars' geological history.

"While the specific formation mechanism of the MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones remains unknown, this is still one of the most exciting findings to date," Murphy said.

Organic Carbon Survives Just Beneath Mars' Harsh Surface

One of the most striking results concerns where the organic carbon was found. The material survived only a few microns below the exposed Martian surface, at a depth smaller than the thickness of a sheet of paper. This is the shallowest detection of macromolecular carbon ever reported on Mars.

That location makes the finding particularly unusual. Mars' surface is exposed to radiation, sunlight, and chemically reactive substances that can break down organic molecules. Scientists would generally expect these conditions to make long-term preservation especially difficult so close to the surface.

"The Martian surface environment includes radiation and chemical oxidants that are destructive to organics, and terrestrial laboratory simulations have shown that the survival time of organics in Martian-like conditions -- especially at or near the surface -- depends on factors such as the type of organic molecule and the surrounding minerals," Murphy said. "The MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones is either resistant to degradation and/or has been sufficiently shielded by other minerals, such as clays, or iron-rich Martian soil."

In other words, the carbon may have survived because of its own chemical durability, protection provided by surrounding minerals, or a combination of the two. Understanding how it endured could help scientists determine where similar organic compounds might remain preserved elsewhere on Mars.

Ancient Martian Lakes and Rivers May Have Been Rich in Organic Material

The findings also suggest that organic carbon may not have been confined to a single region of ancient Mars.

Perseverance collected the Bright Angel sample more than 2,000 miles from Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover previously detected organic compounds. Finding organic material at such widely separated locations suggests that the chemistry associated with life's building blocks may once have been common across the Martian landscape.

"It is encouraging for Martian habitability," Murphy said. "This indicates that billions of years ago, organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient lakes and rivers on Mars."

The possibility of widespread organic material is significant because ancient Mars once had environments containing liquid water. If organic compounds were also broadly available, some of those lakes and rivers may have offered important chemical ingredients for life.

However, discovering those ingredients does not mean that living organisms were present. Organic carbon can be produced without biology, and scientists still need to determine exactly how the material in the Bright Angel rocks formed.

Could Martian Rocks Preserve Evidence of Ancient Life?

Determining whether the Bright Angel formation contains fossilized microorganisms remains beyond the capabilities of the rovers currently exploring Mars. Neither Curiosity in Gale Crater nor Perseverance in Jezero Crater carries the large, energy-intensive laboratory equipment needed to conclusively distinguish fossil evidence of ancient life from geological processes.

Perseverance was designed to search for potential biosignatures, including features like those identified in the Cheyava Falls rock. From that perspective, the discovery represents a "resounding win for Mars science," Murphy said.

The next major step would be to examine Martian samples using the more sophisticated instruments available in laboratories on Earth. Such equipment could reveal details too small or chemically subtle for the rover's instruments to resolve, helping researchers determine whether biological processes or nonliving chemistry produced the organic carbon.

If samples from the Bright Angel formation eventually reach Earth, scientists hope to study their minerals and organic compounds with much greater sensitivity and resolution. These investigations could help explain how the macromolecular carbon formed, how it survived, and what its presence reveals about the distribution of organic material across Mars.

Murphy continues to collaborate with the SHERLOC science team as Perseverance explores the Martian surface. Her research also includes studying Earth materials that resemble Martian rocks and using Raman spectroscopy to improve how scientists interpret the measurements returned by the rover.

Murphy's work on SHERLOC Instrument Mars 2020 was supported through JPL Subcontract No. 1641753 to the Planetary Science Institute.

articles.personality_title: NASA’s Perseverance rover finds complex organic carbon in ancient Mars rocks
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wondered if Mars could have supported life. Organic carbon, a key ingredient for life, had been suspected but not confirmed in Martian rocks until now.

**What happened** – NASA’s Perseverance rover used a special instrument called SHERLOC to study rocks in the Bright Angel formation on Mars. It found complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of two ancient rocks, named including one called Cheyava Falls. This carbon is made of large connected atoms, similar to materials found on Earth and in meteorites.

**Impact** – Finding organic carbon so close to Mars’ surface is surprising because radiation and chemicals usually break down these molecules. The discovery shows that organic material might have been widespread in ancient Martian lakes and rivers, not just in one place. This gives scientists new clues about Mars’ environment billions of years ago.

**What’s next step** – Scientists want to bring samples from Mars back to Earth. Using advanced labs, they hope to learn if the organic carbon came from living things or nonliving chemistry. This could help answer if life ever existed on Mars.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Perseverance’s discovery of complex organic carbon near the Martian surface reveals that the building blocks of life were likely common on ancient Mars and sets the stage for future sample analysis on Earth.

articles.title: I Am Artemis Katie Spicer
articles.summary: For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history. Spicer works in the […]
articles.content:
For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history.

NASA’s Katie Spicer stands in front of the crew cabin prototype for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lunar lander. The lander is one of two commercial human landing systems that will help safely ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for the agency’s crewed Artemis missions in 2028. NASA/Bill Strafford

Spicer works in the Flight Operations Directorate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she evaluates and monitors design and development of Blue Origin’s lander. The design of the Blue Moon lander is rapidly evolving as Blue Origin continues to develop a streamlined lander test article for the agency’s Artemis III rendezvous and docking mission in low Earth orbit as well as a fully functional lander for a crewed lunar landing in 2028.

Spicer works closely with her NASA and Blue Origin counterparts to ensure the design of the Blue Moon lander can support the overall Artemis mission objectives.

“I look at the design of everything Artemis crews will touch, work with, or interface with to ensure systems will function the way crews will need them to,” Spicer said. “In some cases, the design might meet requirements, but I delve deeper into details. How easy will it be for crew to grab handles or handrails? Can they operate push-button displays in microgravity? Are the hygiene systems as user-friendly as possible in the limited space that’s available in the spacecraft? And, are there proper procedures and training to ensure the crew can safely and effectively use the systems? Evaluating all these operational details with crew perspective is part of my job.”

Spicer has spent her career looking at the small details in the big picture.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in microbiology from the Pennsylvania State University in State College, Spicer spent several years working as a full-time homemaker and raising three children. She got her start at NASA working part-time in the historic Life Sciences Laboratory, performing duties such as washing dishes, cleaning lab equipment, and running tests for scientists.

“I went from tidying up and keeping my home running to maintaining the historic lab where the Apollo crews were quarantined when they came back from the Moon and the Moon rock samples were stored,” Spicer said.

From there, Spicer began working with science payloads on the space station. She helped operate the Human Research Facility racks in the International Space Station National Laboratory and worked with scientists and crew to ensure in-flight processes and protocols were completed. It was there that Spicer found a love for the fast-paced dynamic of real-time space operations.

Spicer became a flight controller at NASA Johnson’s Mission Control Center in 2018. The learning curve to become a flight controller was steep, but it did not deter her. Spicer studied and trained for five years to earn the ultimate instructor and flight controller certifications.

“Unlike most people I work with, I don’t have an engineering degree,” Spicer said. “On my own, I studied engineering principles. I passed boards and certification tests. I learned to speak ‘engineer!’”

Spicer spent five years as an Operations and Support Officer in the space station’s flight control room in Mission Control, also known as the “front room” to spaceflight.

Now, when she looks at the Moon in the night sky, Spicer says she’s humbled and honored to be part of the team that’s sending astronauts back to the lunar surface.

“I’m reminded of the great responsibility that NASA has in this endeavor, of the legacy of the courageous Apollo crews who went before, and inspiring the next generation of space explorers to keep going and reaching for the stars!” she said.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

To learn more about the Artemis program, visit:

https://www.nasa.gov/artemis

articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA is preparing to send astronauts back to the Moon through its Artemis program, aiming for a crewed lunar landing by 2028. One important part of this mission is the Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, developed by Blue Origin, which will carry astronauts from lunar orbit down to the Moon’s surface.

**What happened** – Katie Spicer, who works at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, is the lead for integrating the Blue Moon lander. She checks every detail of the lander’s design to make sure astronauts can use it safely and easily. Spicer began her NASA career in a supporting role and worked her way up to become a flight controller and now leads this critical project.

**Impact** – Spicer’s work is unique because she focuses on how astronauts will actually live and work inside the lander, not just the technical parts. She makes sure things like handles, buttons, and hygiene systems are easy to use in space. Her role helps ensure the Artemis missions will succeed and astronauts will be safe on the Moon.

**What’s next step** – The Blue Moon lander will continue to be tested and improved as NASA prepares for the Artemis III mission in 2028. Spicer and her team will keep working closely with Blue Origin to get the lander ready for astronauts to use.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Katie Spicer’s careful work on the Blue Moon lander helps make NASA’s goal of returning humans to the Moon safer and more achievable.

articles.title: A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time
articles.summary: Autonomous in-orbit manufacturing will be key to any future space economy, and researchers have taken the first step with a robot building a radio antenna without astronaut assistance
articles.content:
Autonomous in-orbit manufacturing will be key to any future space economy, and researchers have taken the first step with a robot building a radio antenna without astronaut assistance

Artwork showing how a robot might autonomously construct a structure in space DARPA/Colie Wertz

A robot has built a structure in space without any help of astronauts. The first-of-its-kind achievement is a step towards autonomous in-orbit manufacturing and assembly of structures such as space stations and data centres, which will be crucial if we want to develop an orbital economy.

Sergio Pellegrino at the California Institute of Technology and his team developed their robot as part of a US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) initiative to explore new ways to build in space. Large orbiting structures in the past have either been assembled with the help of astronauts or launched pre-assembled and folded up, spring-loaded to unfold upon release from their capsules.

But unfolding doesn’t work for more complex structures, and sending astronauts to build space stations isn’t cost-effective. “We’ve been unfolding things in space, there’s been a lot of unfolding,” says Pellegrino. “The big picture is how are we going to transition from unfolding in space to building in space.”

Advertisement

The robot that he and his team built is essentially a sophisticated arm that picks up parts and clicks them together in a process similar to putting up a tent or playing with a toy construction set. The precision involved in the movements makes this more difficult than one might expect, especially because the researchers only had 18 months to take the whole project from idea to execution in orbit.

Since its March launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the robot has been working on building a radio antenna, 1.4 metres in diameter, from a set of tubes, joints and reflective nets. As it went along, images of each step were beamed back to Earth, where the researchers checked them and troubleshot any problems with an identical robot in their lab. Construction of the antenna hasn’t quite been completed and the mission ends in December, but work has proceeded far enough to prove that this is a viable approach, says Pellegrino.

Free newsletter Sign up to Launchpad Sign up to newsletter

Now that it has had its first test, Pellegrino hopes that other researchers and space-flight businesses get onboard to accelerate development of faster, larger assembly systems. “I think our objective should be that in the next 5 years we start doing some of this, and in 10 years, there is the beginning for a real maturing infrastructure,” he says.

Eventually, the goal is to build much larger structures, with less troubleshooting from the ground.

Taking space-based construction out of human hands could accelerate the development of businesses and science in orbit enormously, and putting together one radio antenna in space is just the beginning.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant technological breakthrough with a robot autonomously assembling a structure in space, marking a major step toward in-orbit manufacturing and the development of a future space economy. This achievement has broad implications for space exploration, infrastructure, and commercial activities in orbit, and it is well-detailed with context and future goals.
articles.personality_title: Robot builds first structure in space without human help
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In the past, large space structures were either launched already built or assembled by astronauts in space. Building complex structures this way is difficult and expensive, so scientists have been looking for new methods.

**What happened** – A robot developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology, as part of a US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) project, has successfully assembled a radio antenna in orbit without any astronaut assistance. Launched in March from California, the robot used an arm to connect parts like tubes and nets to form a 1.4-meter-wide antenna.

**Impact** – This is the first time a robot has built a structure in space on its own, showing that autonomous manufacturing is possible. This method could save money and effort by reducing the need for astronauts to build things in orbit. It also opens the door for creating larger and more complex space structures in the future.

**What's next step** – The current mission ends in December, but researchers plan to improve the robot’s abilities and encourage other teams to develop faster and bigger space-building systems. The goal is to start regular in-orbit construction in about five years and create a mature space infrastructure within ten years.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, a robot has built a structure in space by itself, marking a key step toward future space manufacturing and building larger orbiting facilities.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un robot construit la première structure dans l’espace sans aide humaine
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Jusqu’à présent, les grandes structures spatiales étaient soit lancées déjà assemblées, soit montées par des astronautes dans l’espace. Construire des structures complexes de cette manière est difficile et coûteux, les scientifiques cherchent donc de nouvelles méthodes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un robot développé par des chercheurs du California Institute of Technology, dans le cadre d’un projet de la DARPA (Agence américaine pour les projets de recherche avancée de défense), a réussi à assembler une antenne radio en orbite sans l’aide d’astronautes. Lancé en mars depuis la Californie, le robot a utilisé un bras pour connecter des pièces comme des tubes et des filets et construire une antenne de 1,4 mètre de diamètre.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois qu’un robot construit seul une structure dans l’espace, prouvant que la fabrication autonome est possible. Cette méthode pourrait économiser de l’argent et des efforts en réduisant le besoin d’astronautes pour monter des structures en orbite. Elle ouvre aussi la voie à la création de structures spatiales plus grandes et plus complexes.

**Prochaine étape** – La mission actuelle se termine en décembre, mais les chercheurs prévoient d’améliorer les capacités du robot et d’encourager d’autres équipes à développer des systèmes de construction spatiale plus rapides et plus grands. L’objectif est de commencer une construction régulière en orbite d’ici cinq ans et de créer une infrastructure spatiale mature dans dix ans.

**Une phrase clé** – Pour la première fois, un robot a construit seul une structure dans l’espace, marquant une étape importante vers la fabrication spatiale et la construction de grandes installations en orbite.
articles.personality_title_es: Un robot construye la primera estructura en el espacio sin ayuda humana
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hasta ahora, las grandes estructuras espaciales se lanzaban ya armadas o eran ensambladas por astronautas en el espacio. Construir estructuras complejas de esta forma es difícil y caro, por lo que los científicos buscan nuevas maneras.

**Qué pasó** – Un robot desarrollado por investigadores del Instituto de Tecnología de California, como parte de un proyecto de la Agencia de Proyectos de Investigación Avanzada de Defensa (DARPA) de EE.UU., ha ensamblado con éxito una antena de radio en órbita sin ayuda de astronautas. Lanzado en marzo desde California, el robot usó un brazo para conectar piezas como tubos y redes y formar una antena de 1,4 metros de ancho.

**Impacto** – Esta es la primera vez que un robot construye una estructura en el espacio por sí solo, demostrando que la fabricación autónoma es posible. Este método podría ahorrar dinero y esfuerzo al reducir la necesidad de astronautas para construir en órbita. También abre la puerta para crear estructuras espaciales más grandes y complejas en el futuro.

**Próximo paso** – La misión actual termina en diciembre, pero los investigadores planean mejorar las habilidades del robot y animar a otros equipos a desarrollar sistemas de construcción espacial más rápidos y grandes. El objetivo es empezar la construcción regular en órbita en unos cinco años y crear una infraestructura espacial madura en diez años.

**Una frase clave** – Por primera vez, un robot ha construido una estructura en el espacio por sí mismo, marcando un paso clave hacia la fabricación espacial y la construcción de grandes instalaciones orbitales.
